bodyMarkdown:
## Electrical Engineering Salary: From Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

When you're working out an **electrical engineering salary**, the starting point is often an hourly rate. Whether you're a contractor, a casual employee, or a full-time worker under the *Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award 2020* (the Electrical Award), understanding how to convert that hourly figure into annual, fortnightly, and weekly amounts is essential. This guide uses the latest Fair Work Ombudsman rates and the Australian Taxation Office tax scales to give you a clear picture.

### The Basic Calculation: Hourly × Hours × 52

The standard formula for an annual salary from an hourly rate is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For full-time employees under the Electrical Award, ordinary hours are an average of 38 per week (). So if your hourly rate is $27.53 (the Grade 1 minimum including industry allowance), your annual pay would be:

$27.53 × 38 × 52 = $54,399.28

That's your gross income before tax and before super. If you're paid fortnightly, simply double the weekly figure: $27.53 × 38 = $1,046.14 per week, so $2,092.28 per fortnight.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 for a 38-hour week. But the Electrical Award sets higher minimums. For example, an Electrical worker Grade 1 (the entry-level classification) must receive at least $27.53 per hour when you include the industry allowance (). Higher grades pay more: a Grade 5 electrician with a licence allowance earns $32.19 per hour, and a Grade 10 reaches $39.97 per hour.

If you're a casual employee, you get a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. For Grade 1, that's $27.53 × 1.25 = $34.41 per hour. The loading compensates for not receiving paid leave or notice of termination. You can use our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page to see how this affects your take-home pay.

### Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Your employer must contribute superannuation at 12% of your ordinary earnings (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830). This is paid *on top* of your salary, not deducted from it. So if your annual gross is $54,399, your employer adds $6,528 in super. That brings the total employment cost to $60,927. For more on how super interacts with your pay, see [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Tax and Medicare

Once you have your annual gross, you can estimate tax using the 2026–27 resident rates:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). For a $54,399 salary, tax would be approximately $7,867 and Medicare $1,088, leaving about $45,444 after tax. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a personalised estimate.

### What This Means for Your Electrical Engineering Salary

The rates above are minimums. Many electrical engineers and technicians earn well above the award, especially if they hold licences, work in specialised fields, or have experience. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70 in May 2026, which equates to about $108,352 per year. That's roughly $54.82 per hour for a 38-hour week. So an electrical engineering salary can be significantly higher than the award floor.

When you're negotiating or comparing offers, always check whether the rate includes allowances (like tool or licence allowances) and whether super is quoted separately. Our [reference tables](/data) provide a full breakdown of award classifications and rates.

### Using the Timesheet Tool

To quickly convert any hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, or weekly figures, use [the timesheet](/). Simply enter your base hourly rate, and if you're a casual, tick the box to add 25% loading. The tool does the rest, applying the standard 38-hour week and showing you the gross amounts. Remember, the calculator assumes no overtime, penalties, or salary sacrifice – it's a starting point for your budget.

### Summary

- Annual gross = hourly rate × 38 × 52
- Fortnightly gross = weekly × 2
- Award minimums (Electrical Award) are higher than the National Minimum Wage
- Casual loading adds 25% on top of the ordinary rate
- Super is 12% paid on top, up to the contribution cap
- Tax and Medicare reduce your take-home pay

For more details on award pay guides, visit [pay guides](/blog). And if you're comparing different job offers, our [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page can help you weigh up hourly rates against salaries.
